passage:
Tuesday
The coaching institute's ad was everywhere today: "95% of our students placed!" and a wall of smiling faces. Lokesh has already paid the deposit. I almost did too.
But at the counselling desk I asked: 95% of whom? Turns out it's 95% of students who finished and sat the final test. How many joined? The man at the desk got vague. Lokesh's senior told us half the batch dropped out by month three. So maybe it's more like half of half.
Not saying it's bad. Maybe it's great. But before I pay anything, I'm going to find five people who joined and didn't finish, and ask them what happened.
Shankar

qa.q: What did the coaching institute's ad say?
qa.a: 95% of our students placed, with a wall of smiling faces.

qa.q: Why did Shankar ask '95% of whom?'
qa.a: Shankar felt doubtful that the smiling faces showed everyone, suspecting they were only those who finished, and wanted to know about everyone who joined.

qa.q: What makes Shankar's plan a sensible one?
qa.a: Talking to five people who joined and didn't finish shows the whole group, including the missing ones, before any money is paid.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel after hearing Shankar's questions?
qa.a: Lokesh, who already paid the deposit, might feel uneasy or defensive, but also prompted to ask what happened to the dropouts.

grounding: Someone in their mid-twenties asks what the full batch looked like, including dropouts, before trusting a course's success figure.

passage: At the panchayat meeting in Dhanauri, a seed dealer pointed to three farmers in the front row. "All three used our new wheat seed, and all three doubled their harvest!" Heads nodded. Shreya, the young agriculture extension worker, raised her hand. "How many farmers in the block bought this seed last season?" The dealer hesitated. "Around forty." "And the other thirty-seven?" Nazia, a farmer at the back, called out, "My field had the same seed. Half of it failed." Two more hands went up. Shreya kept her voice friendly. "Maybe it's a good seed. But before the panchayat praises it, let's hear from all forty, and check whose fields had canal water." The dealer's smile tightened. The three in the front row shifted in their seats.

qa.q: How many farmers bought the new seed last season, according to the dealer?
qa.a: Around forty.

qa.q: Why did Shreya ask about the other thirty-seven?
qa.a: Shreya felt doubtful that the three in the front row told the whole story, and wanted to see the whole group before praising the seed.

qa.q: What does Shreya propose the panchayat do next?
qa.a: Hear from all forty farmers and check whose fields had canal water before praising the seed.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel when Shreya's question gives her a chance to speak?
qa.a: Nazia, whose field half failed, may feel relieved that her loss finally counts in the story.

grounding: A young extension worker asks about all the farmers who used a seed, not just the three winners, before it is praised.

passage:
At the Copenhagen running club's Tuesday meeting, the coach pinned up photos of five members who'd run marathons under three hours. "All five used my twelve-week plan," she said. "It works."
Everyone clapped. Anders, twenty-five, raised a hand. "How many people started the plan?"
The coach blinked. "Around forty last year."
"And the other thirty-five?"
There was a pause. Emil, beside him, whispered, "Mate, don't ruin it."
"I'm not," Anders said quietly. "I want to join. I just want to know what happened to everyone else."
The coach checked her notes. Twelve had dropped out injured. Eight had finished slower than before. The rest had improved a little.
"So it helps some people," Anders said, "and hurts some. That's useful to know." He signed up, but asked for the injury-prevention sessions too.

qa.q: How many people started the plan last year, according to the coach?
qa.a: Around forty last year.

qa.q: What did Anders want when he asked about the other thirty-five?
qa.a: He wanted to know what happened to everyone who tried the plan, not only the five winners, because he was genuinely interested in joining and wanted the full picture.

qa.q: How did asking about the missing runners change Anders's choice?
qa.a: Learning that twelve had dropped out injured led him to sign up but also ask for the injury-prevention sessions.

qa.q: How might Emil see Anders's question at first?
qa.a: Emil seems embarrassed at first, thinking Anders is spoiling the celebration, not seeing that the question helps everyone decide sensibly.

grounding: It shows a thoughtful person asking about all who tried a training method, including those who failed, before praising it.

passage:
At the staff meeting of the Pune secondary school, the principal held up three board exam toppers' photos. "All three attended Mr. Gokhale's weekend crash course. I'm proposing every Class 10 student joins next year."
Heads nodded. Irawati, a second-year maths teacher, looked at the photos, then raised her hand. "How many students attended in total?"
Asif, the admissions clerk, checked. "Sixty-two."
"And how did the other fifty-nine do?"
The room went quiet. Asif pulled up the marks. Some had improved, some had dropped, and many were unchanged. Two parents had complained their children were exhausted.
"Maybe it helps some students," Irawati said. "I'd like to know which ones before we make it compulsory. And the three toppers were already scoring high in Class 9."
The principal frowned, then nodded. "Asif, get me the full list, before and after."

qa.q: How many students attended the crash course in total?
qa.a: Sixty-two.

qa.q: Why did Irawati raise her hand after seeing the photos?
qa.a: She felt that three toppers alone didn't show whether the course worked, and wanted to see the whole group before praising it.

qa.q: What did Irawati's questions lead the principal to decide?
qa.a: The principal asked Asif for the full list of marks before and after, instead of making the course compulsory straight away.

qa.q: How might the parents who complained feel if the course became compulsory?
qa.a: They would probably feel ignored, since their children found it exhausting and their experience would have been hidden behind the three toppers' photos.

grounding: It shows a teacher asking what happened to all the students who took a course, not only the toppers, before praising it.

passage:
Dear Farhan,
Thanks for sending the brochure for the data-science bootcamp. I can see why you're excited: those six alumni stories are impressive, and one of them now works at a big firm.
Before we recommend it to our juniors, though, I'd like to ask the bootcamp a few questions. How many people started in each batch? How many finished? Of those, how many found jobs in data within a year? The brochure shows six faces, but it doesn't say whether they're six out of twenty or six out of six hundred.
If the numbers look good, I'll happily be the first to sign our juniors up. If they won't share them, that tells us something too.
Shall I write to them tomorrow?
Ishita

qa.q: How many alumni stories does the brochure show?
qa.a: Six.

qa.q: Why does Ishita want to ask questions before recommending the bootcamp?
qa.a: Ishita feels cautious, because six impressive faces don't show whether they're six out of twenty or six out of six hundred.

qa.q: Which questions does Ishita want answered, and why do they matter?
qa.a: How many started, finished and found data jobs within a year, because only the whole batch shows whether the course really works.

qa.q: How might Farhan feel reading the email?
qa.a: Farhan might feel slightly deflated but respected, since the excitement is acknowledged and a fair next step is offered.

grounding: A young professional asks for the whole batch's results before praising a course that advertises only its success stories.

passage: Tenzin, people ask why Seema, the agriculture officer, didn't just push the new mulching method everywhere after the success stories. Here's why. The company brought us five farmers who had doubled their yields. Five beautiful fields, great photos. The officers around me were ready to print posters. But I asked, "How many farmers tried it in total?" Silence. Then someone admitted it was sixty-two. So I asked to see the other fifty-seven. Some had average results. Many had lost crops, because the method needs water they didn't have. The five were all near the canal. If I had looked only at the winners, I'd have sent the method to dry villages and ruined a season. Now I always ask the same thing first: who's missing from this picture?

qa.q: How many farmers had tried the method in total?
qa.a: Sixty-two.

qa.q: How did Seema feel when the other officers wanted to print posters?
qa.a: Seema felt cautious and a little uneasy, sensing that five photos couldn't show the whole picture.

qa.q: What question did Seema ask, and what did it reveal?
qa.a: How many farmers tried it in total; it revealed fifty-seven others, many of whom lost crops without canal water.

qa.q: What would change for farmers in dry villages if Seema had not asked?
qa.a: They might have been pushed into a method that needs water they didn't have, and lost a season's crops.

grounding: A young officer asks how many farmers tried a method and what happened to the rest before praising it.

passage: I'm Pema, and I teach in the room next to Jasleen's, so I was at the staff meeting when the principal held up the results. "The five students who used the new revision app all scored above ninety. We should make it compulsory." Everyone nodded. Jasleen raised her hand. "Ma'am, how many students used the app in total?" The principal checked. Forty. "And the other thirty-five?" Nobody knew. Jasleen offered to find out. Over the next week I saw her in the staff room every lunch with the class registers, adding columns. The other thirty-five had scored just like everyone else. The five toppers had always been toppers. At the next meeting, the principal thanked her and said the app would stay optional. I can't say what Jasleen felt, but she was smiling as she packed up the registers.

qa.q: How many students had used the app in total?
qa.a: Forty.

qa.q: What might Jasleen's smile suggest?
qa.a: She probably felt satisfied and relieved that the full picture was seen before the app was made compulsory.

qa.q: What did Jasleen do before accepting the praise for the app?
qa.a: She asked how many used it in total and what happened to the other thirty-five, then checked the registers.

qa.q: How did the principal react to Jasleen's findings?
qa.a: The principal thanked her and kept the app optional instead of compulsory.

grounding: A colleague describes a young teacher asking about the students missing from a success story before a method is praised.

passage:
Monday. The bootcamp's website was full of smiling alumni: "From teacher to software engineer in 12 weeks!" Pema was tempted. Jomon, her flatmate, had already signed up. "Look at them all," he said.
Wednesday. Before paying, Pema emailed the bootcamp: "How many people started your last three batches, how many finished, and how many got developer jobs within six months?" She also found a forum of past students.
The following Tuesday. The bootcamp sent a vague reply about "many success stories." The forum was clearer: out of one batch of ninety, about thirty finished, and around fifteen got developer jobs. Several said they'd been left in debt. Pema didn't sign up. She looked for a cheaper evening course with published numbers, and asked Jomon, gently, if he had seen the forum.

qa.q: How many people from the batch of ninety got developer jobs, according to the forum?
qa.a: Around fifteen got developer jobs.

qa.q: Why did Pema email the bootcamp before paying?
qa.a: She felt tempted but cautious, wanting to know about everyone who started, not only the smiling alumni on the website.

qa.q: What would you advise someone choosing a course with glowing success stories?
qa.a: Ask, as Pema did, how many started, how many finished and how many reached the promised result, and look for past students' own accounts.

qa.q: How might Jomon feel when Pema asks if he has seen the forum?
qa.a: Jomon might feel uneasy or defensive, having already signed up based on the alumni photos alone.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful person asking where the dropouts and failures are before trusting a course's success stories.

passage: Damini, you're asking whether to follow that fitness trainer everyone's praising? Let your Aditi Mausi tell you about my first job, at an ad agency in Mumbai. Our boss came back from a conference with a new method. "All the top agencies use it," he said, showing us three famous campaigns. Everyone clapped. I was twenty-four and I wanted to clap too. Instead I asked, in a very small voice, "Which agencies tried it and didn't do well?" The room went quiet. He didn't know. So I spent a weekend calling people I knew at other firms. Four had tried it. Three had dropped it within a year; it cost too much time. Only the successes had made it to the conference. We tried a small version on one client instead. The boss never thanked me. But we didn't lose a year.

qa.q: How many of the four firms Aditi called had dropped the method within a year?
qa.a: Three had dropped it within a year.

qa.q: What was young Aditi feeling when she asked her question in the meeting?
qa.a: She felt nervous, asking in a very small voice, because everyone else was clapping.

qa.q: Which choice in the story saved the agency a year?
qa.a: Calling other firms to find out who had tried the method and failed, then trying only a small version on one client.

qa.q: How might the boss have felt when the room went quiet?
qa.a: The boss was probably embarrassed and a little irritated, having shown only the famous successes without knowing about the failures.

grounding: An elder recalls asking which firms had failed with a method before praising it, and finding that only the successes were visible.

passage: The vendor needed an answer by five. Their sales rep had shown Mohit, the new operations manager at the logistics firm, a slide of glowing case studies: seven companies that had cut delivery times using the new routing software. Mohit's boss had already said, "Looks good, sign it." It was 3:30 and the warehouse was noisy with the evening shift. Urmila, from finance, leaned over. "Seven is a lot." "Seven out of how many?" Mohit said. He called the rep. "How many clients do you have in total, and how many cancelled in the first year?" A long pause. "We have about sixty. Around twenty didn't renew." Mohit asked for two names from the twenty. At 4:45 he called one of them: the software hadn't worked with their older scanners, like his. He wrote to his boss: "Let's test it at one warehouse first."

qa.q: How many clients did the vendor have in total?
qa.a: About sixty, and around twenty didn't renew.

qa.q: What might Mohit have been feeling when his boss said "sign it"?
qa.a: He was likely uneasy and cautious, feeling pressure to agree but doubting that seven glowing case studies told the whole story.

qa.q: What did Mohit do that helped under time pressure?
qa.a: He asked how many clients had cancelled, called one of them, and proposed a one-warehouse test instead of signing straight away.

qa.q: How might Urmila see the case-study slide at first?
qa.a: Urmila was impressed by seven successes, seeing them as a lot before anyone asked how many others had failed.

grounding: Shows a manager under time pressure asking where the failures are before trusting a vendor's success stories.

passage:
The poster in the Pune office canteen said: "20 of our graduates now work at top tech firms!" Yusuf was sold. "I'm signing up for this coding bootcamp," he told Ishita. "Look at the results."

Ishita, who worked in HR, read the poster twice. "Twenty. Out of how many?"

"Does it matter?"

"It really does. If twenty joined, that's amazing. If two thousand joined, that's one percent."

Yusuf looked it up. The bootcamp didn't say. He emailed them. The reply was vague: "Many hundreds of students."

"And what happened to the rest?" Ishita asked. "Where are the ones who didn't get jobs? Are they on any poster?"

Yusuf sighed. "No."

"I'm not saying don't go," Ishita said. "Just ask to speak to a few random graduates, not the ones on the poster."

He wrote that down.

qa.q: How many graduates did the poster say worked at top firms?
qa.a: 20 of our graduates now work at top tech firms!

qa.q: What was Ishita feeling as she read the poster twice?
qa.a: Ishita felt doubtful and curious, wondering what the whole group looked like before praising the bootcamp.

qa.q: What did Ishita suggest, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Ishita suggested asking how many joined and speaking to random graduates, so the failures become visible before deciding.

qa.q: How might Yusuf feel after the vague email reply?
qa.a: Yusuf probably felt disappointed and more cautious, noticing the bootcamp was hiding the full picture.

grounding: A thoughtful HR worker asks how many joined a bootcamp and where the failures are before praising its results.

passage:
"Tenzin, you have to read this. Every startup in this accelerator raised money!"

"Every one, Rashmi?"

"Look. Fifteen success stories. All of them on the website."

"How many startups joined in total?"

"It doesn't say."

"Hmm. Can we find out?"

Rashmi searched. An old news article: "Accelerator welcomes 120 startups."

"So fifteen out of a hundred and twenty."

"Oh."

"And where are the other hundred and five?"

"Not on the website."

"Right. The website only shows the ones that survived."

"So it's not a bad programme?"

"Maybe it's good. Maybe not. We just can't tell from the winners alone."

"What should we do?"

"Talk to some of the ones that didn't make it. See what happened."

Rashmi opened a new tab. "I'm finding the list of all hundred and twenty."

qa.q: How many startups joined the accelerator in total?
qa.a: Accelerator welcomes 120 startups.

qa.q: How did Rashmi feel on seeing the real total?
qa.a: Rashmi felt surprised and a bit deflated, realising the fifteen stories were only a small part of the whole.

qa.q: What did Tenzin suggest to judge the programme fairly?
qa.a: Tenzin suggested finding the full list and talking to startups that didn't make it, rather than judging only by the winners.

qa.q: How might the accelerator see Rashmi's questions?
qa.a: The accelerator might prefer people only see the success stories, so honest questions could make them uncomfortable.

grounding: A thoughtful person asks where the failures are and how many joined before praising an accelerator.

passage:
I'm Manoj, and I run operations at a small logistics firm. Last month my boss wanted to copy a competitor's strategy: cut prices by half for three months to grab customers. "It worked for SpeedMove," he said. "They're huge now."

I asked something that made the room go quiet: "How many companies tried the same thing and went under?"

Nobody knew. So Pranav, our analyst, looked it up over the next week. He found eleven other firms in the region that had tried heavy price cuts in the last five years. Two survived. Nine closed or were sold cheaply.

"We only remember SpeedMove because it survived," Pranav said. "The others aren't around to tell their story."

My boss was annoyed at first. But he looked at the list for a long time.

We didn't copy the strategy. We tested a small discount in one city instead.

qa.q: How many of the eleven other firms survived?
qa.a: Two survived.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when asking the question in the meeting?
qa.a: Manoj seemed cautious and curious, wanting to know about the failures before praising the strategy, even though it made the room go quiet.

qa.q: What did Manoj and Pranav do that led to a better decision?
qa.a: They looked for everyone who tried the strategy, not just the survivor, and then tested a small discount instead of copying it.

qa.q: How might the boss have felt looking at the list?
qa.a: The boss was annoyed at first, then probably thoughtful and a bit relieved to have avoided a risky move.

grounding: A thoughtful worker asks how many firms tried a strategy and failed before praising one survivor's success.

passage:
Supervisor's note, 3 July
Minakshi came in excited about a tuition centre that wanted our scholarship partnership: its brochure showed forty smiling toppers from last year. Nandini, who reviews our partners, read it twice and asked a quiet question: "Forty toppers out of how many students? And where are the rest?" Minakshi admitted she didn't know. Nandini wrote to the centre asking for the full batch results, including students who left mid-year. The reply took two weeks: the batch had started with over four hundred, and nearly a third had left before the exam. We didn't reject the centre, but we asked for a small trial with our own students, tracking every one of them. I've asked Nandini to add "Who is missing?" to our partner checklist.

qa.q: How many toppers did the brochure show?
qa.a: Forty smiling toppers from last year.

qa.q: What does Nandini's quiet question suggest about her state of mind?
qa.a: She seems curious and calmly cautious, not swept up by the smiling faces, wanting to see the whole group before feeling impressed.

qa.q: Why was asking for the full batch results a wise step?
qa.a: It showed that the batch began with over four hundred and nearly a third left, so the forty toppers were a small, selected part of the story.

qa.q: How might Minakshi feel after the centre's reply?
qa.a: Minakshi may feel a little embarrassed about the early excitement, but also glad the team checked before committing.

grounding: Shows a thoughtful person asking where the failures are and what the whole group looked like before praising a course.
